cultural.summary: Resistant peas are the strongest weapon you have!
cultural.how: Palam Sumool is the resistant check at Palampur; Him Palam Matar-1 is reported moderately resistant. Palam Priya and Pb-89 are only moderately susceptible and Azad P-1 is susceptible.
cultural.evidence: CSK HPKV Palampur 48-genotype screen. Him Palam Matar-1 is snippet-level; check nursery availability.

cultural.how: Sow in October-November in the low and mid hills (end of October gave the highest yields at Palampur) and April-May in the high hills. Avoid late sowing and late-maturing varieties.
cultural.evidence: UHF Nauni pea economics paper; Palampur sowing-date study (snippet).

cultural.summary: Airy, staked plants and clean fields get less mildew!
cultural.how: Grow peas on stakes (bower system), burn infected pea stubble after harvest, do not sow next to last season's stubble, and remove volunteer pea plants.

botanical.summary: A mineral spray that cut mildew by about half in a Mandi trial!
botanical.how: Spray wettable sulphur at 0.2% (2 g per litre of water) at the first white specks, covering both sides of the leaves.
botanical.evidence: Mandi (HP) trial: about 54% disease control. The paper's treatment labels are inconsistent, so treat the figure as approximate.

natural_farming.how: Spray jeevamrit diluted to 10% (1 L in 9 L water) on the plants every 14 days, or drench at 10-20% at 14-15 day intervals.
natural_farming.evidence: UHF Nauni pea nutrition studies (snippets) used 10-20% jeevamrit at 14-15 day intervals. These are yield trials; no natural-farming input has disease-control data on pea. A Palampur trial found natural-farming pea yields of 72-78 q/ha against 206-212 q/ha conventional.

details.what_it_does: Builds soil microbial life. Traditionally credited with suppressing fungal and bacterial diseases, but this is not quantified.
materials_needed: A handful of undisturbed bund/forest soil
preparation_steps: Mix all ingredients in a 200 L drum and make up to 200 L with water.
Cover with a cloth or gunny bag and keep in shade.
Stir clockwise morning and evening.
Ready after 48 hours.
application_steps: Dilute 1 part strained jeevamrit with 9 parts water (10%).
Spray in the evening or drench near the roots every 14-15 days.
Use soon after it is ready.
safety_notes: Do not apply on waterlogged soil.

cultural.summary: Orange pustules underneath, not white powder!
cultural.how: Rust gives orange-brown pustules mostly on the underside of leaves, and the spores come off as yellow powder. It likes 20-25 C with dews and rain; dry hot weather slows it. Take a photo of the underside.

cultural.summary: The rust waits on old debris!
cultural.how: Destroy all diseased plant debris after harvest, rotate with non-leguminous crops and try mixed cropping.

cultural.summary: Be realistic: natural options are limited here!
cultural.how: No natural spray with pea rust data was found. Rely on sanitation, rotation and spacing, and ask your KVK if pustules spread fast in humid weather.
cultural.evidence: Searched NIPHM, UHF Nauni and CSK HPKV sources.

cultural.summary: The disease is seed- and debris-borne!
cultural.how: Use healthy certified seed, space plants for airflow, and remove and burn diseased plants soon after you see purplish-brown flecks on the lower leaves and stems.
cultural.evidence: NIPHM AESA package (national, not HP-specific). Listed in the national package as a Himalayan-region disease.

cultural.summary: Old plant debris carries the disease to the next crop!
cultural.how: Remove and burn (or bury deep) diseased plants and crop debris after harvest, and rotate with crops from a different family.

cultural.summary: Be realistic: natural options are limited here!
cultural.how: No natural spray with Ascochyta data on pea was found. The disease is worst in wet weather and when plants lodge, so staking and sanitation matter most.
cultural.evidence: Searched NIPHM and HP sources; a Kumaon trial found foliar bioagent sprays did not reduce leaf blight.

cultural.summary: The grubs live inside the leaf!
cultural.how: Pick and destroy leaves with winding white mines early. Severe infestation can cause large yield loss; in HP more than 20% avoidable loss was reported beyond 40% infestation.

biological.summary: Tiny parasitic wasps already work for you!
biological.how: Diglyphus and Opius wasps parasitised 15-20% of leaf miners in natural-input plots against 2-7% in synthetic-spray plots, so avoid broad-spectrum insecticides.

botanical.summary: Best-documented natural spray for leaf miner in HP!
botanical.how: Soak 100 g dried neem (or Melia/Bakain) drupes per litre of water (10%), strain, and spray three times.
botanical.evidence: Palampur trial on var. Lincoln: leaf miner numbers fell about 59.5% and leaflet infestation about 38%, against about 51% for a synthetic. Cow urine 5% was the weakest treatment.

natural_farming.how: Spray Agniastra at 5% (5 L strained Agniastra in 100 L water) when mines first appear.
natural_farming.frequency: At first mines; repeat after 10 days
natural_farming.evidence: A Neri (HP) thesis (snippet) ranked Agniastra 5% second among treatments for pea leaf miner, behind spinosad. Percentages were not retrieved.

details.what_it_does: Used against sucking insects, small caterpillars and pod/fruit borers.
preparation_steps: Mix all ingredients in the cow urine.
Boil on a low flame with the lid on.
Leave 48 hours, stirring morning and evening.
Strain through cloth.
application_steps: Dilute 5 L of strained Agniastra in 100 L water (5%).
Test on a few plants first.
Spray in early morning or evening and repeat after 10 days if needed.
safety_notes: Wear gloves, mask and eye protection: the chilli and tobacco irritate skin and eyes.
Keep out of reach of children and animals.
Tobacco can carry tobacco mosaic virus: on capsicum, chilli, brinjal and tomato prefer Neemastra or Brahmastra, or make it without tobacco, and wash hands well after handling tobacco.

cultural.summary: Aphids cluster on new shoots and under tender leaves!
cultural.how: Look for curled, pale, sticky leaves with sooty mould. Aphids breed about a week per generation, so act early. Conserve ladybirds, lacewings and syrphid flies.

biological.how: Release 4,000 green lacewing larvae per acre.
Hang 4-5 yellow sticky traps per acre just above the crop.

cultural.summary: Leaves alone can mislead: look at the roots!
cultural.how: Fusarium wilt: yellowing of lower leaves, drooping cotyledons, leaflet margins curling in 3-5 week plants, brown inside the stem. Root rot: reddish-brown to black streaks on roots and a girdled lower stem. White rot: whitish shredded stem with hard black bodies.

cultural.summary: These fungi live in the soil for years!
cultural.how: Rotate with non-leguminous crops, avoid waterlogging, do deep summer ploughing, and solarize with clear polythene for about 25 days before sowing. Remove and burn diseased plants early.
cultural.evidence: NIPHM pea package. In dry-temperate NW Himalaya surveys, root rot averaged 34% and white rot 8.4% (snippet). A Lahaul project note suggests replacing root-rot-prone pea with capsicum or tomato.

cultural.how: Treat seed with Rhizobium culture at 250 g per acre of seed before sowing.

biological.summary: A friendly fungus guards the seedling roots!
biological.how: Treat seed with Trichoderma viride at 4 g per kg seed (0.4%).
biological.evidence: Kumaon (non-HP) pea trial: best treatment, wilt 4.7%. NIPHM also advises Trichoderma-treated FYM at field preparation but prints no quantity.
